# Giftedness as Two Measurements: Where You Start, and How Fast You Improve

**What it is** — Issurin presents a practical, "dual approach" to identifying gifted
youngsters, attributed to Bril (1980) with his own modifications. It splits giftedness
into two components (Figure 4.11, PDF p. 164, printed p. 153; **verified against the
page image**): **predisposition to a certain activity**, which determines the athlete's
**initial level** of relevant fitness (speed, endurance, agility, etc.), and
**trainability**, which determines the **improvement rate** during initial preparation.
The diagram also names two confounds feeding into those same two outcomes:
**previous experience** (prior training, test familiarity) feeds initial level alongside
predisposition, and **preparation quality** feeds improvement rate alongside
trainability. Issurin states this directly as a limitation, using a worked illustration
(PDF p. 165, printed p. 154): testing eight-year-olds' swimming fitness, "the behavior
of these children in water will be very different and previous experiences will affect
the results much more strongly than the children's real predisposition to competitive
swimming," because some children already have aquatic experience with parents,
others have had a few lessons, and others none at all. Similarly, improvement rate
"depends not only on an individual's trainability but also on the quality of the
preparation. This becomes evident when comparing the progress of athletes who train
under different conditions with different coaches. However, for athletes training in
one group with the same coach, improvement rate adequately reflects trainability"
(PDF p. 165, printed p. 154). So improvement rate reflects trainability only for athletes
training in one group with the same coach; across different coaches and conditions it
also reflects preparation quality.

Combining the two axes gives a three-by-three grid, initial level (High, Medium, Low)
on the left and improvement rate (High, Medium, Low) on the right, joined by seven
labelled links (Figure 4.12, PDF p. 166, printed p. 155; page image; based on Bril 1980
and the author's modifications): High-High "very gifted"; both High/Medium crossings
(High initial with Medium rate, and Medium initial with High rate) "gifted";
Medium-Medium "ordinary gifted"; both Medium/Low crossings "moderately gifted";
Low-Low "not gifted". High/Low combinations (either direction) have no link and are
not graded. The book's
text: "This method of diagnosis was first implemented in team and dual sports mostly
because of practical needs (Bril, 1980)" (PDF p. 165, printed p. 154); Bril (1980) is
*Selection in ball games* (reference list, PDF p. 169, printed p. 158).

Issurin gives explicit, sport-type-differentiated guidance on how long an evaluation
period needs to be to read improvement rate reliably (PDF pp. 166-167, printed pp.
155-156, six points, quoted/paraphrased): (1) absolute unsuitability for a sport (e.g.
"tall and heavy candidates in gymnastics; small children in basketball") can be
recognized quickly; (2) non-gifted candidates are usually recognizable within "about
three-four months" of short-term preliminary preparation; (3) diagnosing giftedness
in maximal speed and power sports needs "a relatively short period... usually... up to
one year"; (4) in highly coordinated sports (gymnastics, figure skating), identification is
limited by the earlier initial-preparation window itself and "takes between 1-2 years";
(5) in team and dual sports, where systematic preparation starts later, very gifted
athletes "can be identified faster (two-three months) but this process usually takes
about one year" (the book's point 5 cross-references "Figure 7.8", sic, which should
read Figure 4.8); (6) "perhaps the longest period for giftedness identification is needed
in endurance sports, where many world-level athletes are recognized as potential elite
athletes after three-four years of systematic preparation."

**Why it works** — The framework's internal logic (separating a starting-point
measure from a rate-of-change measure, and naming the confounds on each) is the
author's own stated reasoning. Inference: that separation is methodologically sound as
a testing design principle. **The author gives no outcome data** validating
that athletes graded "very gifted" by this grid go on to elite performance at
higher rates than those graded lower; the six-point duration guidance is presented as
practical experience-based judgment, not derived from a cited study with a stated
sample.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** directly usable as a testing-design principle for any
Applied Performance evaluation of prospective or first-year athletes: separate an
athlete's **starting-point** test score from their **rate of improvement** over a defined
evaluation window, and explicitly track (rather than ignore) how much of the starting
score is explained by prior training exposure versus untrained predisposition. The
sport-type duration guidance (short window for speed/power sports, longer for
technically complex or endurance sports) is a citable reference point for how long a
true-freshman evaluation period should reasonably run before drawing conclusions
about developmental trajectory, and directly supports keeping "trainability" judgments
provisional during a player's first months in the program rather than fixed at
arrival.

**When NOT to apply** — The dual approach was first implemented in team and dual
sports (Bril, 1980, *Selection in ball games*); the book's duration guidance covers
speed-power, highly coordinated, team/dual and endurance sports. None of it is
football-specific, and the author gives no validation data. **Inference, population
caveat:** the method depends on isolating "quality of preparation" (same coach, same
group) to make the improvement-rate reading meaningful, which the book itself makes
the condition (PDF p. 165, printed p. 154). That is harder to guarantee in a
large-roster college setting with multiple position coaches and strength staff.

**Example** — **Inference:** a true-freshman evaluation protocol that records each
player's testing-day starting values (with a note on prior training background,
per the swimming illustration above) separately from their improvement rate across
the first off-season, and treats "trainability" as unresolved until that improvement-rate
window has actually elapsed, rather than reading it off the initial test alone.

[[case-study--troup-swimmers-maturation-timing-and-longevity]],
[[case-study--sozin-canoe-kayak-age-14-15-performance-benchmark]].

14	# The Quadrennial Cycle: Four Generic Year-Directions, Individualized by Stage Objectives
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin frames multi-year planning around the four-year Olympic
17	cycle, triggered by post-Games analysis: "the challenge of post-Olympic analysis is to
18	internalize positive experiences and reveal the reasons for sub-par performances. Based
19	on the findings, a new preparatory plan is worked out" (PDF p. 143, printed p. 132).
20	He gives a worked example: the Russian national gymnastics team's quadrennial cycle,
21	subdivided into **eight half-year stages**, each with its own general objective (PDF p.
22	144, printed p. 133, cited to Arkajev & Suchilin, 2004): (1) enhancement of
23	sport-specific motor fitness; (2) acquisition of new, highly complex technical skills and
24	their hybrids; (3) updating of competition combinations; (4) further increases in
25	sport-specific motor fitness; (5) enhancement of technical mastery and attaining stable
26	performances; (6) increase in performance quality, stability and stress tolerance; (7)
27	final compilation of competition combinations, endurance for an entire program, and
28	selection of a duplicate Olympic squad; (8) modeling expected competitive conditions,
29	attaining high competitive reliability, and final selection of the Olympic team. Issurin
30	is explicit that this eight-stage division is sport-specific ("a matter of professional
31	competence" depending on conditions), and that "the division of the quadrennial cycle
32	into four annual cycles is the most popular" in general (PDF p. 144, printed p. 133).
33	
34	For the four-annual-cycle version, Table 4.4 (PDF p. 144, printed p. 133; verified
35	against the page image) gives generic year-by-year directions, irrespective of sport:
36	**Year 1**: engagement and examination of new candidates, selection of coaches and
37	staff, updating/correcting training means and methods, remodeling the training
38	repertory, forming team spirit and camaraderie; **Year 2**: further candidate selection
39	and approval, acquisition of new techno-tactical skills, increased training workloads,
40	improved training quality; **Year 3**: attaining maximal training-workload level,
41	approving the Olympic-season annual cycle, determining individual performance
42	characteristics per team member; **Year 4**: stabilizing team make-up (usually with a
43	double Olympic squad), stabilizing workloads at the prior year's level, and approving
44	and stabilizing competitive behavior and performance. Issurin states the third and
45	fourth years "should be very similar since coaches simulate the annual pre-Olympic
46	training design one year before" the Games, though "the training workload level in the
47	pre-Olympic season is usually higher than the year before for various reasons,"
48	including "greater motivation, better conditions for training and restoration, greater
49	budgets" (PDF p. 146, printed p. 135). Inference: "pre-Olympic season" is read here as
50	the fourth year, the season that ends at the Games.
51	
52	**The book states year 4 two ways; both are recorded.** Table 4.4 says year 4 stabilizes
53	workloads "on the level of the preceding year" (PDF p. 144, printed p. 133). The text
54	says the pre-Olympic season's workload is usually higher than the year before (PDF p.
55	146, printed p. 135), and Figure 4.5 plots both athlete groups rising from year III to
56	the Games (experienced about 8.6 to 9.0, younger about 9.7 to 10.0, in "referring
57	units"; PDF p. 145, printed p. 134). The book does not reconcile the two.
58	
59	**Why it works** — The author gives no controlled-comparison mechanism for why
60	this generic four-year sequence outperforms an alternative structure; it is presented as
61	observed common practice ("the division of the quadrennial cycle into four annual
62	cycles is the most popular"). Inference: the table's order reads as squad-building logic
63	(candidate selection and cohesion before workload escalation, workload escalation
64	before stabilization); Issurin gives no such rationale (PDF p. 144, printed p. 133).
65	**Inference:** the underlying logic parallels this library's existing
66	long-term athletic development material: building foundational capacity (team
67	identity, basic skill acquisition) before layering higher, more specific workloads, but
68	Issurin does not state that connection explicitly in this passage.
69	
70	**When to apply** — **Inference:** college football has no
71	literal Olympic quadrennium, but the four-year (or five-year, with a redshirt) eligibility
72	window is a structurally similar bounded multi-year cycle with its own roster-cohort
73	logic: Year 1 (true freshman/transfer intake) mapping to Table 4.4's Year 1 emphasis on
74	candidate evaluation and cultural integration; Years 2-3 to skill/technical acquisition
75	and rising training-workload tolerance; a "walk year" (senior or draft-eligible year)
76	to Table 4.4's Year 4 emphasis on stabilized, individualized performance. The
77	gymnastics eight-stage example is a useful illustration that objective-setting per stage
78	should be concrete and sport-specific rather than generic, which is directly usable
79	guidance for building a position-group or class-cohort development plan.
80	
81	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference, population caveat:** both the eight-stage
82	gymnastics example and the four-year Table 4.4 are drawn from Olympic individual/
83	team-technical sports with a single fixed quadrennial target and squad continuity
84	controlled by national-team selection, not from a college roster with annual signing
85	classes, transfer portal turnover, and no shared four-year entry cohort (a program's
86	"Year 1" and "Year 4" athletes are present simultaneously every season, unlike a
87	national team's cycle-wide cohort). The table's per-year directions are the author's own
88	applied synthesis of common practice, not a study with an outcome measure; no
89	evidence is given that following this sequence produces better long-term results than
90	an alternative one. The Table 4.4 vs Fig. 4.5 age-cohort content (older/experienced vs.
91	younger-athlete workload differentiation within this same quadrennial frame) is
92	treated separately in
93	[[heuristic--older-vs-younger-athlete-quadrennial-workload-differentiation]].
94	
95	**Example** — **Inference:** a position group's four-year development plan borrowing
96	Table 4.4's shape: Year 1 focused on evaluating and culturally onboarding new signees
97	and transfers; Year 2 on techno-tactical (scheme/position) skill acquisition and raising
98	training-load tolerance; Year 3 on maximizing training workload and identifying each
99	player's individual performance profile; Year 4 on stabilizing role, workload, and
100	game-performance consistency for players entering their final season or a likely draft
101	evaluation.
102	
103	**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/framework--ltad-sequential-model]],
104	[[heuristic--older-vs-younger-athlete-quadrennial-workload-differentiation]],
105	[[framework--long-term-preparation-four-stage-model-and-directions]].

12	---
13	
14	# Building the Annual Plan: A Nine-Step Sequence, Anchored on Target Competitions
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin gives a fixed nine-step sequence for constructing an annual
17	program (Table 4.2, PDF p. 138, printed p. 127), illustrated stepwise in Figures 4.1-4.4
18	(PDF pp. 139-141, printed pp. 128-130; verified against the page images): (1) determine
19	the target and mandatory competitions, normally taken from the international/national/
20	regional calendar; (2) determine the terms and duration of training stages and periods
21	("in terms of target competitions and methodology"); (3) divide training stages into
22	several meso- and microcycles; (4) plan additional competitions and trials to "finalize
23	the training stages and to diversify the preparatory program"; (5) plan training camps
24	(objectives, terms, places), which also covers altitude preparation (Ch. 5); (6) plan
25	medical and sport-specific tests, with the initial medical exam early season; (7)
26	calculate integrative workload characteristics per month (total mileage, number of
27	lifts, throws, etc.); (8) calculate the same for the full annual cycle, compared against
28	previous years to reveal "weak" points; (9) correct the plan following that review ("as
29	a rule, the first version needs correction and this operation is obligatory"). Figures
30	4.1-4.4 plot competitions on four levels against a month-by-month grid that fills in
31	stages/periods, meso/microcycles and training camps in the later figures as each step
32	is completed. Figure 4.1 places the national championship (NCh) as the Level A target,
33	the national cup (NCup) at Level B, and the winter cup (WC) and regional trials (RT) at
34	Level C (caption: "targeted (level A) and mandatory competitions (Levels B and C)").
35	Level D is empty in Figures 4.1-4.2 and is filled only in Figures 4.3-4.4, with the
36	dotted arrows of the additional competitions and trials planned at step 4 (PDF pp.
37	139-141, printed pp. 128-130). The **optimal design places important competitions at the end of a
38	training stage** (Fig. 4.2 caption, PDF p. 139, printed p. 128). The plan is not
39	considered final at step 9: "it must first be reviewed by the administration, colleagues
40	and athletes and with repeated analysis, will lead to corrections" (PDF p. 141, printed
41	p. 130) before it "receives the final version status that is used for realization."
42	
43	Layered on this procedure is a seasonal content trend (Table 4.3, PDF p. 142, printed p.
44	131; verified against the page image): early season favors continuous/uniform/
45	alternating methods in the accumulation mesocycle and a wide range of fitness
46	exercises, more individual workouts, and general restorative means (stretching,
47	relaxation, low-intensity aerobics); mid-season narrows toward interval methods, a
48	restricted exercise range, and adds physiotherapy/massage/mental training/nutritional
49	supplements; late season is "strictly programmed interval exercises" in both
50	accumulation and transmutation mesocycles, mostly specialized exercises, strictly
51	programmed workouts, and the "most effective individually selected restorative
52	means." The sixth row, use of competitive simulation forms, runs "Periodically, not
53	frequently" early season, "Systematically, more frequently" mid-season, and "Higher
54	contribution in training program" late season. The general rule: "training stages within the annual cycle should be similar
55	but not identical," with mid- and especially late-season stages "more rigorous, more
56	strictly programmed and better managed" (PDF p. 142, printed p. 131).
57	
58	Issurin also assigns competition an explicit developmental role even early in the
59	season, for three stated reasons (PDF p. 143, printed p. 132): it completes each
60	training stage as "a compulsory component of the training program"; it "breaks the
61	usual routine and brings out the very important element of athlete spirit"; and it
62	"provides athletes with extraordinary training stimuli that can not be obtained from
63	regular workloads." The competitive program itself should be diversified early season,
64	narrowed toward event-specific standards mid-season, and strictly event-specific late
65	season.
66	
67	**Why it works** — The author's own stated rationale for reserving the most rigorous,
68	best-managed workloads for the pre-competition stages is two-part (PDF p. 142,
69	printed p. 131): physiologically, it "gives the benefit of higher training responses
70	prior to the most important events"; psychologically, "it heightens the athletes'
71	self-confidence as they know that they have additional reserves during the most
72	stressful phase of their preparation." No further mechanism is given for why the
73	nine-step sequence itself (as opposed to some other ordering) produces a better plan
74	than ad hoc planning; the author states only that "coaches put together annual
75	programs based on their own experience, knowledge and common sense" and that
76	Block Periodization "implies specific demands to planning" without benchmarking the
77	sequence against an alternative (PDF p. 138, printed p. 127).
78	
79	**When to apply** — **Inference:** mapped to a college football calendar, the Level

# Building the Annual Plan: A Nine-Step Sequence, Anchored on Target Competitions

**What it is** — Issurin gives a fixed nine-step sequence for constructing an annual
program (Table 4.2, PDF p. 138, printed p. 127), illustrated stepwise in Figures 4.1-4.4
(PDF pp. 139-141, printed pp. 128-130; verified against the page images): (1) determine
the target and mandatory competitions, normally taken from the international/national/
regional calendar; (2) determine the terms and duration of training stages and periods
("in terms of target competitions and methodology"); (3) divide training stages into
several meso- and microcycles; (4) plan additional competitions and trials to "finalize
the training stages and to diversify the preparatory program"; (5) plan training camps
(objectives, terms, places), which also covers altitude preparation (Ch. 5); (6) plan
medical and sport-specific tests, with the initial medical exam early season; (7)
calculate integrative workload characteristics per month (total mileage, number of
lifts, throws, etc.); (8) calculate the same for the full annual cycle, compared against
previous years to reveal "weak" points; (9) correct the plan following that review ("as
a rule, the first version needs correction and this operation is obligatory"). Figures
4.1-4.4 plot competitions on four levels against a month-by-month grid that fills in
stages/periods, meso/microcycles and training camps in the later figures as each step
is completed. Figure 4.1 places the national championship (NCh) as the Level A target,
the national cup (NCup) at Level B, and the winter cup (WC) and regional trials (RT) at
Level C (caption: "targeted (level A) and mandatory competitions (Levels B and C)").
Level D is empty in Figures 4.1-4.2 and is filled only in Figures 4.3-4.4, with the
dotted arrows of the additional competitions and trials planned at step 4 (PDF pp.
139-141, printed pp. 128-130). The **optimal design places important competitions at the end of a
training stage** (Fig. 4.2 caption, PDF p. 139, printed p. 128). The plan is not
considered final at step 9: "it must first be reviewed by the administration, colleagues
and athletes and with repeated analysis, will lead to corrections" (PDF p. 141, printed
p. 130) before it "receives the final version status that is used for realization."

Layered on this procedure is a seasonal content trend (Table 4.3, PDF p. 142, printed p.
131; verified against the page image): early season favors continuous/uniform/
alternating methods in the accumulation mesocycle and a wide range of fitness
exercises, more individual workouts, and general restorative means (stretching,
relaxation, low-intensity aerobics); mid-season narrows toward interval methods, a
restricted exercise range, and adds physiotherapy/massage/mental training/nutritional
supplements; late season is "strictly programmed interval exercises" in both
accumulation and transmutation mesocycles, mostly specialized exercises, strictly
programmed workouts, and the "most effective individually selected restorative
means." The sixth row, use of competitive simulation forms, runs "Periodically, not
frequently" early season, "Systematically, more frequently" mid-season, and "Higher
contribution in training program" late season. The general rule: "training stages within the annual cycle should be similar
but not identical," with mid- and especially late-season stages "more rigorous, more
strictly programmed and better managed" (PDF p. 142, printed p. 131).

Issurin also assigns competition an explicit developmental role even early in the
season, for three stated reasons (PDF p. 143, printed p. 132): it completes each
training stage as "a compulsory component of the training program"; it "breaks the
usual routine and brings out the very important element of athlete spirit"; and it
"provides athletes with extraordinary training stimuli that can not be obtained from
regular workloads." The competitive program itself should be diversified early season,
narrowed toward event-specific standards mid-season, and strictly event-specific late
season.

**Why it works** — The author's own stated rationale for reserving the most rigorous,
best-managed workloads for the pre-competition stages is two-part (PDF p. 142,
printed p. 131): physiologically, it "gives the benefit of higher training responses
prior to the most important events"; psychologically, "it heightens the athletes'
self-confidence as they know that they have additional reserves during the most
stressful phase of their preparation." No further mechanism is given for why the
nine-step sequence itself (as opposed to some other ordering) produces a better plan
than ad hoc planning; the author states only that "coaches put together annual
programs based on their own experience, knowledge and common sense" and that
Block Periodization "implies specific demands to planning" without benchmarking the
sequence against an alternative (PDF p. 138, printed p. 127).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** mapped to a college football calendar, the Level
A/B/C/D competition tiers map reasonably well onto a football master calendar: Level
A as the postseason target (playoff/bowl window), Level B as rivalry or
conference-championship-implication games, Level C/D as the rest of the regular-season
slate. Step 1 (fix the target and mandatory events) and step 5 (plan camps, including
fall camp) are directly usable planning anchors for Applied Performance's annual
calendar-building work with the sport coaching staff. The step-7/8 "integrative
workload characteristics per month, compared with previous years" is a concrete,
citable structure for what a season-over-season GPS/load report should track. Eric's
baseline: standardized weekly/monthly coach-facing reporting templates do not yet
exist and are named as unfinished Phase 2 work (`method-baseline.md`, Data, technology
and reporting section, line 159). Inference: steps 7-8 are a possible template for that
gap.

**When NOT to apply** — The book presents the sequence as general ("Despite the
variety of training conditions and specificity of different sports," PDF p. 142, printed
p. 131). Inference: its worked example (Figs 4.1-4.4) is an individual-sport calendar
with a single clearly ranked target competition determined well in advance. The
sequence is not derived from any comparative study of planning
methods (no control condition, no outcome data for the sequence itself). **Inference,
population caveat:** college football's postseason destination (which bowl, or which
playoff round) is not known when the annual plan is first built, which weakens step 1's
premise that the target competition can be fixed at the top of the sequence the way an
Olympic Trials date or a World Championship date can be; the plan has to accommodate
a moving Level-A target rather than a scheduled one. The "optimal design places
important competitions at the end of a training stage" (Fig. 4.2) also assumes the coach
controls stage boundaries around the competition calendar; in football the
competition calendar (one game almost every week, in season) is closer to Issurin's
"competitive microcycle" pattern described elsewhere in this book than to a plan with
discrete preparation stages ending in isolated target events.

**Example** — **Inference:** using the nine-step sequence as a working checklist for a
Baylor football annual calendar: fix the bowl/playoff-window target and the
conference-championship-implication games (step 1); block out fall camp, the
regular-season in-season maintenance stage, and the bowl-prep stage (step 2-3); slot
non-conference "trial" games and any scrimmages (step 4); place fall camp and any
summer training windows (step 5); align the pre-participation physical and preseason
testing battery to early season (step 6); build a month-by-month GPS/load-volume
summary (step 7-8) and review it against the prior season before finalizing (step 9).

13	
14	# Klementiev: Training Volume Fell for 19 Years While Podium Results Kept Coming
15	
16	**What it is** — A single-athlete, 19-year longitudinal case: Ivan Klementiev, USSR
17	then Latvian Olympic canoeist, competed across four Olympic cycles, earning one gold
18	and two silver Olympic medals and seven World Championship golds (PDF p. 148,
19	printed p. 137). His total annual paddling volume was tracked by age (Figure 4.6, PDF
20	p. 149, printed p. 138; page image: the chart's peak at age 21,
21	roughly 4,800 km, matches the text's "maximal training volume was attained at age 21
22	when he trained with the USSR national squad"; volume then oscillates with periodic
23	late-quadrennial upticks but trends down through the following years, with the lowest
24	point at age 37, about 1,500 km). Issurin quantifies the decline by quadrennial-cycle
25	average, relative to the first cycle as 100%: **ages 21-24 = 100%; ages 25-28 = 88.2%;
26	ages 29-32 = 77.4%; ages 33-36 = 61%** (PDF p. 148, printed p. 137; text quote).
27	The author attributes the volume reduction partly to transition periods: "Reduction of
28	the annual training volume is partly conditioned by longer transition periods that
29	increased from one to three months during his career" (PDF p. 148, printed p. 137).
30	Despite the steady volume decline, "after age 30 [he] won four gold medals
31	at the World Championships and two Olympic silver medals" (PDF p. 149, printed p.
32	138). Issurin's own conclusion opens with a hedge: "Apparently, workload reduction was
33	effectively compensated for by a higher quality of training" (PDF p. 149, printed p.
34	138), which he associates with the athlete's own account
35	(Klementiev, 1994) of "better preparation exploiting Block Periodization, a more
36	conscious and effective selection of exercises, avoidance of non-compatible workload
37	combinations, constant attention to restoration, and the use of a logical program of
38	competition." One deviation in the late-quadrennial volume upticks is flagged as
39	non-methodological: in 1984, "because of political, not methodological circumstances,"
40	Klementiev raced a substitute regatta of socialist countries in July instead of the Los
41	Angeles Olympics in August, and "the season was cut short by one month" (text, PDF p.
42	148, printed p. 137). The Figure 4.6 caption records only that at age 24 he "competed
43	in a regatta of socialist countries as an alternative to the Los Angeles Olympic Games"
44	(PDF p. 149, printed p. 138).
45	
46	**Why it works** — The author's own causal claim ("Apparently, workload reduction
47	was effectively compensated for by a higher quality of training") is stated, not
48	demonstrated: no comparison group, no measured "training quality" variable, and no
49	separation of the Block Periodization approach from the other listed factors (exercise
50	selection, compatibility management, restoration, competition-program logic). The one
51	partial cause the author does give for the volume decline itself is the lengthening
52	transition period (one to three months). **The author gives no mechanism**
53	connecting reduced kilometers specifically to Block Periodization. Inference: other
54	explanations for late-career success are not ruled out, including accumulated
55	technical/tactical experience and a selection effect (an athlete who stays competitive
56	to age 36 across four Olympiads is, by construction, one of the rare athletes for whom
57	this pattern worked).
58	
59	**When to apply** — **Inference:** mapped to a college context, useful as a
60	citable, named-athlete illustration that declining training volume is not, by itself,
61	evidence of declining performance capacity in an experienced athlete, and that
62	tracking quality/specificity of training rather than raw volume may be the more
63	relevant monitoring question for a veteran player. Pairs directly with
64	[[heuristic--older-vs-younger-athlete-quadrennial-workload-differentiation]]'s Table
65	4.5 claim that "motor potential doesn't increase but can be utilized more effectively."
66	
67	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** This is an n = 1, uncontrolled,
68	retrospective case with no comparison athlete who trained at a constant or rising
69	volume across the same span. Inference: it cannot separate the effect of reduced
70	volume, Block Periodization specifically, accumulated technical mastery, opponent
71	turnover, or survivorship (only athletes who remained competitive despite aging appear in this kind
72	of retrospective record; athletes for whom volume reduction did not work are absent
73	from it by definition). It is also a single elite paddler in an individual, cyclic-endurance
74	Olympic sport with a fixed quadrennial target; nothing here generalizes to a college
75	football roster's age range (18-23), position-specific demands, or annual (not
76	quadrennial) competitive cycle. Do not cite this case as evidence that reducing training
77	volume improves or preserves performance in general.
78	
79	**Example** — **Inference:** when a program has a small number of veteran players
80	whose measured training volumes are trending down year over year, Klementiev's case
81	is a reason to check training quality, technical execution, and competition-readiness
82	markers before treating the volume decline itself as a red flag, rather than a license to
83	assume volume reduction is automatically beneficial.
84	
85	**Related** — [[heuristic--older-vs-younger-athlete-quadrennial-workload-differentiation]].
86

13	
14	# Four Stages of Long-Term Preparation, Dosed by Hours and Broken Out by Domain
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin gives a four-stage long-term development model. Bompa's
17	entry in this library ([[periodization--bompa/framework--ltad-sequential-model]]) is a
18	three-tier pyramid (multilateral, specialized, high performance) covering the same
19	progression. Issurin adds two things Bompa's entry does not have: an explicit dosing
20	table and a domain-by-domain (technical/physical/tactical/mental) content breakdown
21	per stage. He opens by
22	scoping the topic down: "the athletic career... is highly dependent on the earlier period
23	of long-term preparation that usually begins in childhood. The purview of this chapter
24	restricts consideration of this matter, which is worthy of its own book" (PDF p. 152,
25	printed p. 141). Table 4.6, "based on Issurin, 1994" (PDF p. 152, printed p. 141; page
26	image), gives, per stage: **Preliminary preparation**: 1-3
27	years, 3-4 workouts/week, 45-60 min/workout, 120-170 hours/year; **Initial
28	specialization**: 2-3 years, 4-5 workouts/week, 75-90 min/workout, 250-300
29	hours/year; **Advanced specialization**: 2-3 years, 6-9 workouts/week, 60-120
30	min/workout, 500-750 hours/year; **Sports perfection**: duration "individually
31	dependent," 6-12 workouts/week, 70-150 min/workout, 750-1400 hours/year. Figure 4.8 (PDF p.
32	153, printed p. 142; page image) gives "favorable ages to start systematic preparation":
33	gymnastics and figure skating roughly 7-9; swimming roughly 9-11; team/dual sports
34	("ball games"), weightlifting and fencing roughly 11-14; T&F sprint roughly 11-13;
35	kayaking roughly 12-15; rowing roughly 13-16; T&F marathon roughly 14-17; triathlon
36	roughly 13-18 (adapted from Platonov & Sakhnovsky, 1988, with limits updated from
37	interviews with international experts). Issurin notes a trend toward earlier starts,
38	driven by child-scaled equipment, better training conditions, media popularization, and
39	visible early-starting stars. His example: a few decades ago boys were to begin
40	weightlifting "no younger than age 14"; now "the general practice worldwide is for
41	schoolboys to take part in international weightlifting competitions at age 11 and even
42	earlier" (PDF p. 153, printed p. 142). Juniors with serious swimming experience entering
43	triathlon need about one year of preliminary preparation to acquire cycling and running
44	skills, and the Figure 4.8 data "reflect worldwide practice but do not include special
45	situations in which youngsters begin their training earlier or later" (PDF pp. 153-154,
46	printed pp. 142-143).
47	
48	Each stage's content is broken out by four domains in Tables 4.7-4.10 (PDF pp.
49	154-157, printed pp. 143-146): **Preliminary preparation** (Table 4.7): technical:
50	sport-specific and general skill/coordination acquisition; physical: multilateral,
51	all-round development with sport-specific emphasis, raising general training capacity;
52	tactical: acquaintance with basic tactical demands; mental: consolidating interest,
53	forming motivation, "adoption of fundamental moral principles of 'fair play', team
54	spirit." The book's reason for a preliminary stage of about one to two years: "children
55	with lower initial fitness levels may possess higher sensitivity to training stimuli and
56	within a given time may equal or even surpass the leaders," so the stage is needed both
57	to build motivation and "to evaluate the predisposition and innate abilities of
58	newcomers" (PDF p. 154, printed p. 143). **Initial specialization** (Table 4.8): technical: further sport-specific
59	development, selecting the most favorable discipline/event; physical: more specialized
60	motor-ability development, adapting to sport-typical workloads; tactical: deeper rules
61	and tactics knowledge; mental: self-confidence, will power, "consciousness and
62	responsibility." **Advanced specialization** (Table 4.9): technical: attaining effective,
63	individualized technique, eliminating technical drawbacks; physical: further
64	sport-specific motor-ability gains supporting individualized technique; tactical:
65	individualized tactical/techno-tactical formation; mental: motivation toward
66	excellence, emotional control, mental-regulation skill acquisition. Issurin adds a
67	caution here specific to this stage: "despite increased technical and motor abilities,
68	juniors at this stage are still not completely mature and the use of maximal workloads
69	should be restricted. In particular, administration of highly intense anaerobic glycolitic
70	exercises requires complete control because highly qualified juniors can be overly
71	ambitious in their training routines but not experienced enough in self-regulation of
72	metabolic and muscular reactions" (PDF p. 155-156, printed p. 144-145). **Sports
73	perfection** (Table 4.10): technical: further enhancement with individual style;
74	physical: highest sport-specific ability level and its "improved utilization"; tactical:
75	tactical creativity, automatized favorite skills; mental: total commitment, highest
76	self-confidence, mood self-regulation, mental toughness. This fourth stage is "the most
77	variable in duration": "almost twenty years" for career-long stars like Klementiev and
78	Armstrong, "four-seven years" for most high-performance athletes (PDF p. 156, printed
79	p. 145).
80	
81	**A cross-source contradiction worth recording, not silently resolving:** this
82	library's Verkhoshansky/Supertraining entry
83	([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--russian-sport-school-age-guidelines-table]])
84	gives Soviet sport-school starting ages for some of the same sports that are
85	considerably earlier than Issurin's Figure 4.8 bands: women's gymnastics 4-5 vs.
86	Issurin's gymnastics 7-9; swimming 3-7 vs. Issurin's 9-11; weightlifting 10-11 vs.
87	Issurin's 11-14; basketball 7-8 vs. Issurin's ball games 11-14; track and field 6-7 vs.
88	Issurin's T&F sprint 11-13. The two columns also measure different things:
89	Supertraining's is the age "to begin a sport" in Soviet sport schools, while Issurin's is
90	the "favorable age to start systematic preparation" (Figure 4.8 caption). Issurin's own
91	weightlifting note (from "no younger than 14" a few decades ago to international
92	competition at 11 and earlier) shows his ages moving over time (PDF p. 153, printed p.
93	142). The two tables come from different sources (Table 1.2 in Supertraining is
94	unsourced beyond "the Soviet sports-school system"; Figure 4.8 here is adapted from
95	Platonov & Sakhnovsky, 1988, plus later expert interviews) and neither book reconciles
96	the gap. Record both; do not average them into a single number.
97	
98	**Why it works** — Table 4.6 is cited to the author's own earlier work (Issurin,
99	1994); no outcome data are given, and no study compares athletes trained at these
100	hour/frequency bands against alternative bands. **Inference:** the domain-by-domain content sequencing
101	(general before specific, tactical/mental development paced alongside physical)
102	matches this library's existing multilateral-before-specialization rationale
103	([[periodization--bompa/principle--multilateral-before-specialization]]), but that
104	connection is this entry's own synthesis, not stated by Issurin in this passage.

# Four Stages of Long-Term Preparation, Dosed by Hours and Broken Out by Domain

**What it is** — Issurin gives a four-stage long-term development model. Bompa's
entry in this library ([[periodization--bompa/framework--ltad-sequential-model]]) is a
three-tier pyramid (multilateral, specialized, high performance) covering the same
progression. Issurin adds two things Bompa's entry does not have: an explicit dosing
table and a domain-by-domain (technical/physical/tactical/mental) content breakdown
per stage. He opens by
scoping the topic down: "the athletic career... is highly dependent on the earlier period
of long-term preparation that usually begins in childhood. The purview of this chapter
restricts consideration of this matter, which is worthy of its own book" (PDF p. 152,
printed p. 141). Table 4.6, "based on Issurin, 1994" (PDF p. 152, printed p. 141; page
image), gives, per stage: **Preliminary preparation**: 1-3
years, 3-4 workouts/week, 45-60 min/workout, 120-170 hours/year; **Initial
specialization**: 2-3 years, 4-5 workouts/week, 75-90 min/workout, 250-300
hours/year; **Advanced specialization**: 2-3 years, 6-9 workouts/week, 60-120
min/workout, 500-750 hours/year; **Sports perfection**: duration "individually
dependent," 6-12 workouts/week, 70-150 min/workout, 750-1400 hours/year. Figure 4.8 (PDF p.
153, printed p. 142; page image) gives "favorable ages to start systematic preparation":
gymnastics and figure skating roughly 7-9; swimming roughly 9-11; team/dual sports
("ball games"), weightlifting and fencing roughly 11-14; T&F sprint roughly 11-13;
kayaking roughly 12-15; rowing roughly 13-16; T&F marathon roughly 14-17; triathlon
roughly 13-18 (adapted from Platonov & Sakhnovsky, 1988, with limits updated from
interviews with international experts). Issurin notes a trend toward earlier starts,
driven by child-scaled equipment, better training conditions, media popularization, and
visible early-starting stars. His example: a few decades ago boys were to begin
weightlifting "no younger than age 14"; now "the general practice worldwide is for
schoolboys to take part in international weightlifting competitions at age 11 and even
earlier" (PDF p. 153, printed p. 142). Juniors with serious swimming experience entering
triathlon need about one year of preliminary preparation to acquire cycling and running
skills, and the Figure 4.8 data "reflect worldwide practice but do not include special
situations in which youngsters begin their training earlier or later" (PDF pp. 153-154,
printed pp. 142-143).

Each stage's content is broken out by four domains in Tables 4.7-4.10 (PDF pp.
154-157, printed pp. 143-146): **Preliminary preparation** (Table 4.7): technical:
sport-specific and general skill/coordination acquisition; physical: multilateral,
all-round development with sport-specific emphasis, raising general training capacity;
tactical: acquaintance with basic tactical demands; mental: consolidating interest,
forming motivation, "adoption of fundamental moral principles of 'fair play', team
spirit." The book's reason for a preliminary stage of about one to two years: "children
with lower initial fitness levels may possess higher sensitivity to training stimuli and
within a given time may equal or even surpass the leaders," so the stage is needed both
to build motivation and "to evaluate the predisposition and innate abilities of
newcomers" (PDF p. 154, printed p. 143). **Initial specialization** (Table 4.8): technical: further sport-specific
development, selecting the most favorable discipline/event; physical: more specialized
motor-ability development, adapting to sport-typical workloads; tactical: deeper rules
and tactics knowledge; mental: self-confidence, will power, "consciousness and
responsibility." **Advanced specialization** (Table 4.9): technical: attaining effective,
individualized technique, eliminating technical drawbacks; physical: further
sport-specific motor-ability gains supporting individualized technique; tactical:
individualized tactical/techno-tactical formation; mental: motivation toward
excellence, emotional control, mental-regulation skill acquisition. Issurin adds a
caution here specific to this stage: "despite increased technical and motor abilities,
juniors at this stage are still not completely mature and the use of maximal workloads
should be restricted. In particular, administration of highly intense anaerobic glycolitic
exercises requires complete control because highly qualified juniors can be overly
ambitious in their training routines but not experienced enough in self-regulation of
metabolic and muscular reactions" (PDF p. 155-156, printed p. 144-145). **Sports
perfection** (Table 4.10): technical: further enhancement with individual style;
physical: highest sport-specific ability level and its "improved utilization"; tactical:
tactical creativity, automatized favorite skills; mental: total commitment, highest
self-confidence, mood self-regulation, mental toughness. This fourth stage is "the most
variable in duration": "almost twenty years" for career-long stars like Klementiev and
Armstrong, "four-seven years" for most high-performance athletes (PDF p. 156, printed
p. 145).

**A cross-source contradiction worth recording, not silently resolving:** this
library's Verkhoshansky/Supertraining entry
([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--russian-sport-school-age-guidelines-table]])
gives Soviet sport-school starting ages for some of the same sports that are
considerably earlier than Issurin's Figure 4.8 bands: women's gymnastics 4-5 vs.
Issurin's gymnastics 7-9; swimming 3-7 vs. Issurin's 9-11; weightlifting 10-11 vs.
Issurin's 11-14; basketball 7-8 vs. Issurin's ball games 11-14; track and field 6-7 vs.
Issurin's T&F sprint 11-13. The two columns also measure different things:
Supertraining's is the age "to begin a sport" in Soviet sport schools, while Issurin's is
the "favorable age to start systematic preparation" (Figure 4.8 caption). Issurin's own
weightlifting note (from "no younger than 14" a few decades ago to international
competition at 11 and earlier) shows his ages moving over time (PDF p. 153, printed p.
142). The two tables come from different sources (Table 1.2 in Supertraining is
unsourced beyond "the Soviet sports-school system"; Figure 4.8 here is adapted from
Platonov & Sakhnovsky, 1988, plus later expert interviews) and neither book reconciles
the gap. Record both; do not average them into a single number.

**Why it works** — Table 4.6 is cited to the author's own earlier work (Issurin,
1994); no outcome data are given, and no study compares athletes trained at these
hour/frequency bands against alternative bands. **Inference:** the domain-by-domain content sequencing
(general before specific, tactical/mental development paced alongside physical)
matches this library's existing multilateral-before-specialization rationale
([[periodization--bompa/principle--multilateral-before-specialization]]), but that
connection is this entry's own synthesis, not stated by Issurin in this passage.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** mapped to a Baylor context, the domain-by-domain
tables (4.7-4.10) are a usable template for structuring what "developmental content"
means at each career stage of a college program even though college football players
enter well past Issurin's "preliminary preparation" age band: an incoming freshman's
program content (movement-skill consolidation, general work capacity, tactical
acquaintance with the defense/offense) resembles the "initial specialization" /
"advanced specialization" domain mix more than "sports perfection," which better fits
an established starter. The advanced-specialization caution against maximal
anaerobic-glycolytic loading in not-yet-mature, "overly ambitious" young athletes is a
directly relevant caution for redshirt-freshman and true-freshman conditioning design.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference, population caveat:** Table 4.6's specific
hour/frequency bands and Figure 4.8's starting ages are drawn from Olympic individual
and technical sports (gymnastics, swimming, rowing, weightlifting, etc.); American
football is not listed in either this table or the Verkhoshansky comparison table, and no
data source here addresses a contact team sport with a 100+ player roster and
heterogeneous training ages within a single class. The stage-duration bands are the
author's own applied synthesis (cited only to "Issurin, 1994," his own earlier work, not
an independent study), and the domain content lists, while plausible, carry no cited
outcome evidence distinguishing them from an alternative sequencing.

**Example** — **Inference:** using Tables 4.7-4.8's domain content as a checklist for a
true-freshman's first developmental year: technical (movement-pattern competency
before position-specific technique refinement), physical (multilateral work capacity
before narrow specialization), tactical (scheme literacy before disguised assignments),
mental (culture and buy-in before performance-outcome pressure), while applying
Table 4.9's caution against maximal-intensity anaerobic-glycolytic work for players who
are still not fully mature and may be "overly ambitious" relative to their
self-regulation capacity.

[[periodization--bompa/principle--multilateral-before-specialization]],
[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age]],
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--russian-sport-school-age-guidelines-table]],
[[framework--quadrennial-cycle-four-year-directions]].

14	# Four Talent Factors, Graded by How Fixed They Are
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin defines giftedness as "a predisposition to and a higher
17	trainability for a given activity," treated as "genetically transmitted properties of an
18	individual," such that "a gifted child is potentially a talented athlete" (PDF p. 160,
19	printed p. 149). Citing Williams & Franks (1998) and Williams & Reilly (2000), he
20	organizes talent prediction into four factors, each graded by genetic determination
21	(Table 4.11, PDF p. 161, printed p. 150; **verified against the page image**):
22	**Body build and body composition**: body height, extremity length, foot size
23	(strong); shoulder width, thigh circumference, muscle mass (medium); total body fat
24	(low). **Physiological**: alactic anaerobic power, peak blood lactate, space
25	orientation (high); glycolytic anaerobic power, strength endurance/acidity resistance,
26	flexibility (medium). **Psychological**: self-confidence, anxiety control, motivation,
27	concentration (medium-low), citing Plomin et al. (1994) and Saudino (1997) for a
28	partial heritable component. **Sociological**: parental support, socio-economic
29	background, cultural background, coach-child interaction (heredity independent,
30	though the text adds: "this doesn't mean, however, that they can be changed easily if
31	necessary"). Psychological traits are "somewhat inherited (Plomin et al., 1994;
32	Saudino, 1997) and therefore can be altered during preparation" (PDF p. 160, printed p.
33	149). Issurin's practical point in presenting the table this way: "some
34	anthropometrical and physiological variables are highly dependent on heredity and as
35	such, can not be compensated for by other personal traits. Thus, they can restrict
36	progress in a given sport" (PDF p. 160, printed p. 149). Inference: the high-heritability
37	rows work as constraints on which sports an athlete can realistically excel in, while the
38	lower-heritability rows are more open to training and environment; the book itself
39	warns that heredity-independent sociological factors are not necessarily easy to change.
40	The book gives no numeric heritability estimates; Table 4.11 grades each factor only
41	qualitatively (strong, medium, low, high, medium-low, heredity independent).
42	
43	The unchangeable-predictor approach is operationalized through "model
44	characteristics" (Bulgakova, 1986; PDF p. 161, printed p. 150): favorable
45	anthropometric/physiological combinations by age category, built from longitudinal
46	study of a large athlete group where a sub-group reaches elite level (citing Vorontsov
47	et al. 1999 and Falk et al. 2003 as examples of this being done despite its difficulty),
48	or more commonly from cross-sectional studies comparing less- and more-successful
49	youngsters (PDF p. 162, printed p. 151). Issurin flags the model characteristics' central
50	limitation directly: "the main limitation of this evaluation is in the differing levels of
51	maturity of children that are examined to determine giftedness. Children with slower
52	rates of maturation may be found inferior to more mature teammates but may have
53	greater potential for further progress" (PDF p. 161, printed p. 150). Genetic
54	contribution to training response itself is not constant across a career: "Based on the
55	outcomes of studies with young adult twins, it has been found that the contribution of
56	heredity related factors to training response in an endurance program is different for
57	earlier and later stages of preparation. The initial preparation is less dependent on
58	heredity. However, as athletes progress and approach higher workloads, the genetic
59	control of their training response becomes much stronger (Bouchard et al., 2000)."
60	The book adds that this "partly explains why some gifted endurance athletes cannot be
61	effectively recognized at an earlier stage of their preparation" (PDF p. 167, printed p.
62	156). The book cites these twin studies via Bouchard, Wolfarth, Rivera et al. (2000),
63	"Genetic determinants of endurance performance," a review chapter in *Endurance in
64	Sport*, Vol. II of the Encyclopedia of Sports Medicine (reference list, PDF p. 169,
65	printed p. 158); the primary twin studies are not named in the book and were not
66	checked here.
67	
68	**Why it works** — The heredity-grading in Table 4.11 is presented without a
69	citation for individual cells (the surrounding text cites Williams & Franks 1998 and
70	Williams & Reilly 2000 for the four-factor taxonomy); it functions as the author's
71	synthesized taxonomy rather than a reported finding with its own effect sizes. The
72	genetic-control claim is cited to a review chapter (Bouchard et al., 2000), not to a
73	primary twin study.
74	
75	**When to apply** — **Inference:** directly relevant to how Applied Performance and
76	recruiting staff frame "traits we can develop" versus "traits we are selecting for":
77	Table 4.11's strong/medium/low-heritability split is a usable lens for separating
78	recruiting criteria (anthropometrics, alactic power, space orientation: closer to fixed)
79	from developmental targets (glycolytic capacity, strength endurance, flexibility,
80	psychological skills: more trainable), while the maturation-confound caution is a
81	direct argument for tracking training age and biological maturation alongside any
82	"talent" read on a young or first-year athlete, consistent with
83	[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age]].
84	
85	**When NOT to apply** — The cited taxonomy sources are soccer talent-ID papers
86	(Williams & Franks 1998, "Talent identification in soccer"; Williams & Reilly 2000,
87	"Talent identification and development in soccer"; reference list, PDF p. 170, printed
88	p. 159); the chapter's own examples are swimming, canoe-kayak and gymnastics.
89	**Inference, population caveat:** American football's position-specific demands are
90	not addressed, and no cell in Table 4.11 is football-specific. The heritability labels ("strong," "medium," "high," "medium-low") are
91	qualitative and unsourced at the individual-cell level in this passage; treat them as the
92	author's organizing synthesis, not as quantified heritability estimates. The
93	maturation-confound caution applies most directly to youth/pre-collegiate evaluation
94	and is less relevant once an athlete has finished growth, though the same caution about
95	mistaking current-training-age effects for fixed talent still applies to a true freshman.
96	
97	**Example** — **Inference:** using the four-factor split as a talking-point framework
98	when a coach asks whether a trait is coachable: anthropometrics and alactic power
99	profile are closer to "select for, don't expect to build"; strength endurance,
100	flexibility, and psychological-skill factors are closer to "build through training and
101	sport psychology support," while sociological factors (family support, coach-athlete
102	relationship) sit entirely outside a strength staff's typical intervention but are named
103	here as real contributors to development that the book says are heredity independent
104	but not necessarily easy to change.

14	# 35 Elite Soviet Paddlers: What Age-14-15 Performance Looked Like Before They Were Elite
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin cites a retrospective interview study of 35 "world leading
17	canoe-kayak paddlers who took part in the USSR National team and earned medals in
18	the Olympic Games and World Championships within eight years prior to the study"
19	(PDF p. 163, printed p. 152, citing Sozin, 1986). Respondents were interviewed about
20	their official performance results from ages 14-15, "the end of their first year of
21	long-term preparation"; athletes who began preparation later were excluded from the
22	analysis. "The collected data were subjected to statistical analysis and the
23	performance trends of elite paddlers were calculated" (PDF p. 163, printed p. 152); no
24	statistics are reported. Figure 4.10 (PDF p. 163, printed p. 152; page image) plots
25	performance time on a 500-m course by one-year age step (14-15, 15-16, 16-17, 17-18,
26	18-19) for three groups: at 14-15, kayak males about 139 s, kayak females about 146 s,
27	canoeists about 151 s; at 18-19, about 101.5 s, 118.5 s and 119 s. Kayak males are
28	fastest at every step, and kayak females and canoeists track close together. The
29	figure runs to 18-19 although the interview was about official results "from ages
30	14-15"; the book does not say where the later points come from. The book frames the
31	result as
32	a usable historical benchmark rather than a fixed standard: "despite the substantial
33	improvement of paddles and boats in the two decades since this study was conducted,
34	the results achieved by outstanding athletes in the earlier stages of their preparation
35	remain relevant to this day for evaluation of giftedness in today's young athletes" (PDF
36	p. 163, printed p. 152).
37	
38	**Why it works** — **The author gives no mechanism** connecting age-14-15
39	performance time to eventual elite status; the case is presented purely as a descriptive
40	benchmark curve, not as a validated predictive model. The book says the data were
41	"subjected to statistical analysis" but reports no correlation, sensitivity, or
42	false-positive/false-negative rate for using these times to screen today's youngsters. Issurin's own claim that equipment-era changes do not invalidate
43	the benchmark is asserted, not tested against any comparison of era-adjusted times.
44

# 35 Elite Soviet Paddlers: What Age-14-15 Performance Looked Like Before They Were Elite

**What it is** — Issurin cites a retrospective interview study of 35 "world leading
canoe-kayak paddlers who took part in the USSR National team and earned medals in
the Olympic Games and World Championships within eight years prior to the study"
(PDF p. 163, printed p. 152, citing Sozin, 1986). Respondents were interviewed about
their official performance results from ages 14-15, "the end of their first year of
long-term preparation"; athletes who began preparation later were excluded from the
analysis. "The collected data were subjected to statistical analysis and the
performance trends of elite paddlers were calculated" (PDF p. 163, printed p. 152); no
statistics are reported. Figure 4.10 (PDF p. 163, printed p. 152; page image) plots
performance time on a 500-m course by one-year age step (14-15, 15-16, 16-17, 17-18,
18-19) for three groups: at 14-15, kayak males about 139 s, kayak females about 146 s,
canoeists about 151 s; at 18-19, about 101.5 s, 118.5 s and 119 s. Kayak males are
fastest at every step, and kayak females and canoeists track close together. The
figure runs to 18-19 although the interview was about official results "from ages
14-15"; the book does not say where the later points come from. The book frames the
result as
a usable historical benchmark rather than a fixed standard: "despite the substantial
improvement of paddles and boats in the two decades since this study was conducted,
the results achieved by outstanding athletes in the earlier stages of their preparation
remain relevant to this day for evaluation of giftedness in today's young athletes" (PDF
p. 163, printed p. 152).

**Why it works** — **The author gives no mechanism** connecting age-14-15
performance time to eventual elite status; the case is presented purely as a descriptive
benchmark curve, not as a validated predictive model. The book says the data were
"subjected to statistical analysis" but reports no correlation, sensitivity, or
false-positive/false-negative rate for using these times to screen today's youngsters. Issurin's own claim that equipment-era changes do not invalidate
the benchmark is asserted, not tested against any comparison of era-adjusted times.

**When to apply** — The book files this case under "retrospective studies, in which
the development of outstanding athletes is carefully analyzed with respect to
performance trend, changes in body size etc." (PDF p. 162, printed p. 151), an approach
it presents separately from the longitudinal and cross-sectional "model
characteristics" of Bulgakova (1986)
([[framework--athletic-talent-four-factor-heredity-model]]). **Inference:** as a
template, not as transferable numbers, interviewing an already-elite cohort about their
own performance at a fixed early-career age point, to build a reference curve for
today's youngsters, is a reusable talent-identification method independent of the
specific canoe-kayak times.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** This is a retrospective,
survivorship-selected sample: all 35 respondents were already-successful medalists at
the time of interview. Inference: the study therefore cannot say what fraction of
14-15-year-olds with similar performance times failed to reach the same level (no
comparison group of similarly-fast 14-15-year-olds who did not become elite). It is also
sport- and era-specific (Soviet canoe-kayak, single national federation, with the book
noting "substantial improvement of paddles and boats in the two decades since this
study was conducted"; Inference: the medals fall in roughly the late 1970s to
mid-1980s, given the 1986 citation and the "within eight years prior to the study"
window) with no cited data from any other sport or country, and the book's
own claim that "the results... remain relevant to this day" is the author's assertion, not
a re-tested comparison against a current cohort. Do not use the specific second-count
benchmarks as a screening cutoff for any current sport without independent
verification.

**Example** — **Inference:** the method (not the numbers) could be adapted for a
sport Applied Performance evaluates by asking current or recent elite alumni for their
own testing numbers at a fixed early developmental checkpoint (e.g. end of a true
freshman year), building an internal reference curve for how "what elite eventually
looked like at this checkpoint" compares to a current prospect, while explicitly
tracking that such a curve, built only from athletes who succeeded, cannot say how
many similarly-scoring peers did not.

**Related** — [[framework--athletic-talent-four-factor-heredity-model]],
[[heuristic--dual-approach-initial-level-and-improvement-rate-giftedness]],
[[case-study--troup-swimmers-maturation-timing-and-longevity]].

- Training residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue readiness for max-velocity work degrades. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27]
- The head coach's system of play and roster identity (e.g., a "home run hitters" lineup vs. a "steal bases" lineup) is treated as a direct input into whether a team's programming leans toward maximal strength or toward speed/power emphasis. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.16]

## Data, technology and reporting

- The full technology stack: Catapult (GPS), Kitman Labs (central AMS/data store), Perch (camera-based velocity-based training), Polar (heart rate), and the VALD suite — DynaMo, ForceDecks, ForceFrame, Hub, NordBord, SmartSpeed. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
- Kitman Labs is positioned specifically as the cross-technology data store and analysis/visualization layer, distinct from each vendor's own reporting tool (e.g., VALD Hub, OpenField Cloud). **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
- Documented GPS/VALD workflows exist for the full device lifecycle, but Eric's own gap analysis flags them as generic, template-driven, and lacking Baylor-specific detail (serial numbers, storage locations, troubleshooting) except for the Catapult workflow, which has genuine operational depth. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.2]
- Credential/login management is currently placeholder-only in the Playbook; a secure credential-vault protocol is named as needed but not yet implemented. **Explicit (gap, stated as a to-do)** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.8; performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4]
- Standardized weekly/monthly coach-facing reporting templates do not yet exist; building them is named as unfinished Phase 2 work. **Explicit (gap, stated as a to-do)** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Phase 2]
- Tensiomyography (TMG) is part of the toolkit, with a documented setup/operations SOP, but that SOP is headed with the names of a prior Director and Associate Director of Applied Performance (Althoff, Nelson), not Eric, and current active use is unclear from this corpus. **Inferred (legacy document, status unclear)** [technologytemplatesop.md]

## Education and staff development

- HHPR 5355 ("Power, Speed, Agility, & Periodization in Training") is Eric's own graduate-level course, co-taught with Chris Ruf and Michael Wenger; grading is split across two exams (10% and 20%), a group training-plan project (20%), and lecture/lab participation (40%), with a practical (teach-back) component on exams. **Inferred (transcript, syllabus content)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.1]
- A standalone, 16-week Intern Sport Science Curriculum is proposed, deliberately separate from the Playbook so it can be distributed and revised on its own cycle, aligned to the NSCA Essentials of Sport Science (CPSS) textbook, and adapted from a Clemson model to Baylor's own technology stack (ForceDecks, Catapult, ForceFrame, NordBord, DynaMo, Perch, SmartSpeed, Polar) and to include football alongside Olympic-sport examples. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 5]

135
 
 
 
Experienced, more aged athletes continue the quadrennial cycle with a gradual 
increase in training volume, which in any case is usually less than that for their 
younger counterparts. The model for the third annual cycle is based on the Olympic 
year for each category of athletes.  Both aged and younger athletes increase the level 
of their training workloads and approach their maximum. Generally speaking, the 
third and fourth annual cycles should be very similar since coaches simulate the 
annual pre-Olympic training design one year before in order to provide the highest 
quality preparation at the end stage of the quadrennial cycle. In fact, the training 
workload level in the pre-Olympic season is usually higher than the year before for 
various reasons.  This includes greater motivation, better conditions for training and 
restoration, greater budgets etc.  
 
 
Younger athletes, who have not participated in the Olympic Games have 
typical characteristics. After being involved in Olympic preparations, their athletic 
motivation is greatly stimulated and they usually enjoy better training conditions that 
include more training camps, more qualified training partners, sometimes more 
experienced coaches etc. As a result, these athletes substantially increase their training 
workloads in comparison to the previous year. In the second and third annual cycles 
the training workloads continue to rise although at a smaller rate of increase.  
 
 
From a methodological point of view, it is important to predict and plan 
development of the most relevant motor, technical and tactical abilities. For this, it is 
necessary to expand the corresponding model characteristics of these components of 
preparedness with respect to improvement rates during the quadrennial cycle.  
 
4.3  Sport longevity of highly qualified athletes 
 
 
Contemporary sport has many examples of highly successful athletes who 
continue their careers up to and past age thirty. This athletic longevity has been 
affected by many factors, such as high and stable motivation, proper style of behavior, 
improved training methodology, social support, financial stimulation, etc. In regard to 
the training itself, a number of age-related characteristics can be pinpointed 
irrespective of the sport involved (Table 4.5). 
 
=====
133
 
 
Example. The quadrennial cycle of the Russian gymnastics national team is 
subdivided into eight half-year stages.  Each stage is directed to a specific general 
objective:  
1. 
Enhancement of sport-specific motor fitness 
2. 
Acquisition of new, highly complex technical skills and their hybrids 
3. 
Updating of combinations used in competition 
4. 
Further increases in sport-specific motor fitness 
5. 
Enhancement of technical mastery and attaining stable (reliable) performances 
6. 
Increase in performance quality, stability and stress tolerance. 
7. 
Final compilation of competition combinations, development of endurance for 
an entire program and selection of a duplicate Olympic squad 
8. 
Modeling of expected competitive conditions, attaining high competitive 
reliability and final selection of the Olympic National team. 
Each of the above stages encompasses a complex evaluation of the cumulative 
training effect induced by the completed program. 
 
 
This example shows that dividing the quadrennial cycle into separate stages is 
a matter of professional competence and depends on sport-specific conditions. 
Nevertheless, the division of the quadrennial cycle into four annual cycles is the most 
popular. In general, the main directions of quadrennial preparation, irrespective of 
sport, are presented in Table 4.4.

Athletic preparation within a quadrennial cycle 
Year 
Main directions of preparation 
1st 
Engagement and examination of new candidate, selection of coaches and 
other staff specialists, updating and correcting usual training means and 
methods, remodeling training repertory, formation of team spirit and 
camaraderie between athletes and staff. 
2nd 
Further selection and approval of new candidates, acquisition of new techno-
tactical skills, increase in training workloads, improving quality of training 
3rd 
Attaining maximal level of training workloads, approving the annual cycle 
planned for the Olympic season and determining the individual performance 
characteristics for each team member 
4th 
Stabilization of team make-up usually with the double Olympic squad; 
stabilization of workloads on the level of the preceding year, approval and 
stabilization of the competitive behavior and performance

Of course, a number of additional social factors affect the preparation and 
behavior of aged athletes. Very often they combine their athletic preparation with 
professional activity and some odler athletes have families which substantially 
changes their mentality and life priorities. The preparation particulars can be 
illustrated using examples of two outstanding athletes who attained great results 
during their long athletic careers. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
====
137
 
 
Case study of long-term training workloads. The world-famous canoeist, 
Olympic Champion Ivan Klementiev represented the USSR and from 1991, 
Latvia during four Olympic cycles. He earned one gold and two silver 
Olympic medals and seven World Championship gold medals. During a 
period of 19 years many aspects of his training were well documented with 
the most informative being total annual paddling volume (Figure 4.6). 
Analysis of the multi-year annual training volume reveals a number of salient 
points: 
-- Maximal training volume was attained at age 21 when he trained with the 
USSR national squad.  Annual training volume tended to decrease despite 
periodic deviations in the following years; 
-- Quantitative analysis of the average annual volume over quadrennial cycles 
when he took part in the Olympic Games reveals the following: ages 21-24 
– 100%; ages 25-28 -88.2%; ages 29-32 – 77.4%, and ages 33-36 – 61%; 
-- Analysis of periodic oscillations reveals a remarkable increase in training 
volume in the final years of the Olympic cycles with one exception.  In 
1984, because of political, not methodological circumstances – instead of 
competing in the Los Angeles Olympics that was held in August, the athlete 
competed in a substitute regatta of socialist countries held in July.  As a 
result, the season was cut short by one month; 
-- Reduction of the annual training volume is partly conditioned by longer 
transition periods that increased from one to three months during his career.

(USSR, Latvia);  
Key:  OG – Olympic Games, WCh – World Championships, G – gold,  
S – silver, B – bronze medals, at age 24 the athlete competed in a regatta 
of socialist countries as an alternative to the Los Angeles Olympic Games 
 
It should be emphasized that despite the constant decrease in total workloads, 
Ivan Klementiev continued to have extremely successful performances and after age 
30 won four gold medals at the World Championships and two Olympic silver 
medals. Apparently, workload reduction was effectively compensated for by a higher 
quality of training. This training enhancement was associated with better preparation 
exploiting Block Periodization, a more conscious and effective selection of exercises, 
avoidance of non-compatible workload combinations, constant attention to 
restoration, and the use of a logical program of competition (Klementiev, 1994). This 
great athlete earned a Ph.D. degree, and has been a highly successful coach, serving 
on the national canoe squads of Poland and Spain.  
 
As already stated, long-term preparation is characterized by a cumulative 
training effect, in which physiological evaluations are of special interest. 
Unfortunately, such data for multi-year training among elite athletes are very limited.

139
 
 
Therefore, the case study of legendary cyclist Lance Armstrong is unique and 
extremely interesting (Coyle, 2005). 
 
Case study of physiological changes during long-term preparation. Lance 
Armstrong, world famous cyclist, became World Champion and seven-time Grand 
Champion of the Tour de France, the most famous and prestigious road race in the 
world. From ages 21 to 28 he was examined in a physiology laboratory for body 
composition, maximal oxygen uptake, maximal blood lactate and mechanical 
efficiency of pedaling. At age 24 he was diagnosed with testicular cancer and 
during a two year period he came through surgery and treatment that included 
chemotherapy. From ages 27-32 Lance Armstrong was victorious six times in the 
Tour de France, undoubtedly an incredible success in world sport. 
           During a seven year period, starting from age 21, the athlete's body weight 
increased slightly by 0.8 kg while lean body weight increased by 1.1 kg. The 
multi-year trend of physiological variables showed the following (Figure 4.7): 
- 
the maximum oxygen uptake reached peak value at age 23, declined after 
medical treatment and did not reach the highest level until age 28 when he won 
the Tour de France; 
- 
maximum heart rate decreased by 6 beat/min; 
- 
mechanical efficiency, as the ratio of mechanical work to energy expended, 
increased by 8.8%; 
- 
mechanical power obtained at an oxygen uptake of 5.0 l/min displayed a 
substantial increase of 18%. 
It is worth noting that the final estimate of maximum oxygen uptake, 71 
ml/kg/min, is inferior to the data of elite cyclists which approaches the level of 80 
ml/kg/min (Padilla et al., 2000). It can be speculated that when Lance reduced his 
body weight prior to the races, the real level of maximum oxygen uptake per body 
weight became higher than previously. Nevertheless the study findings indicate 
that the individual progress of this great athlete was determined not by 
enlargement of his physiological potential but by its more efficient utilization. The 
physiological mechanism of this improved muscular efficiency is still unclear. 
The hypothetical contributors to such improvement can be associated with 
pronounced hypertrophy and improved contractility of slow muscle fibers, 
alteration in myosin ATPase activity, increased cycling efficiency induced by 
altitude training and enhanced pedaling technique.

It should be noted that Lance Armstrong attained enormous success after 
extremely serious surgery and medical treatment.  His autobiography is an example of 
magnificent athletic and human fortitude (Armstrong, 2000). Of course, his athletic 
career and individual data are unique. In any case, the tendencies revealed in the study 
of Armstrong’s progress are highly typical. Indeed, many highly qualified athletes 
approach their biological limits but continue to attain their best performances and 
even improve their athletic results. The main source of such individual progress is 
usually better utilization of their motor and physiological capabilities. This improved 
utilization can be conditioned by physiological, biomechanical and psychological 
factors, where individual creativity, self-confidence and athletic wisdom play a great 
role.

ages 21 to 28 y. Description of this person is noteworthy for two reasons. The approach of this study will be to report results from standardized laboratory testing on this individual at five time points corresponding to ages 21.1, 21.5, 22.0, 25.9, and 28.2 yr.

The initial preliminary preparation stage is characterized mainly by all-round 
(multilateral), mostly attractive but not excessive workloads, where harmony between 
basic technical and fitness exercises is of utmost importance (Table 4.7). It is 
generally agreed that children with higher level motor abilities have visible benefits in

fitness levels may possess higher sensitivity to training stimuli and within a given 
time may equal or even surpass the leaders.  
 
Therefore, a period of about one-two years of preliminary preparation is 
needed both to strengthen, interest, motivate, instill willingness to continue training in 
a selected sport, and to evaluate the predisposition and innate abilities of newcomers 
for a specific sport. Participation in competition is strongly recommended at this stage 
but in reasonable quantities and using a diversified competitive program. The training 
program as a whole is of great importance for forming and developing proper mental 
abilities that can decisively determine whether long-term preparation will continue.
